newsitem.title: MEXICO: INTERVIEW -PRI says to keep slim congress majority.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW -PRI says to keep slim congress majority.

text.p: Polls show they may be headed for trouble but President Ernesto Zedillo's Institutional Revolutionary Party (PRI) believes it will secure a slim congressional majority in key elections next month, a leading PRI candidate told Reuters.

Arturo Nunez, widely tipped as the PRI's next lower house leader if he wins election as a deputy in his home state of Tabasco, said the PRI was sure it would keep its 68-year-old congressional majority.

Under the complicated voting system for the July 6 elections, 300 of the 500 seats in the Chamber of Deputies (the lower house) will be assigned to winners of district races. The remaining 200 will be shared out by proportional representation.

"The PRI could lose up to 80 (of the 300 districts) but we would also have a right to the proportional representation and that would allow us to suppose we would go on holding an absolute majority," Nunez said in an interview conducted Thursday afternoon.
"Our information, a series of elements we have, gives us the firm conviction that the PRI will continue to keep its absolute majority."

National opinion polls show the PRI just below the 42.2 percent of the vote it needs for a congressional majority but party sources told Reuters they expect a wafer-thin majority. This would probably be smaller than the 20-seat margin it held between 1988 and 1991 -- the PRI's smallest majority to date.

Questioned about how things would work if the PRI failed to secure a lower house majority, Nunez said the extremes of Mexican politics -- ranging from the right-wing PAN to the left-wing PRD -- could make agreement difficult.
"Our political debate is very polarized," he said. "Democracy needs a consensus...where differences are of contrast but we don't discuss basic matters."

As examples of the sharp policy differences between Mexico's main parties, Nunez said: "The PRD wants to reopen agrarian reform and start distributing land again, a policy from the Mexican Revolution now closed by the PRI with the PAN's agreement. In countries like England you are not talking about the regime of property."

"The PAN is bringing up again a debate which other parts of the world ended a long time ago. Religious education in public schools.aThe PAN...virtually wants religious education, something which in the 19th Century divided Mexicans."

Nunez -- who was deputy interior minister until he resigned to fight this year's election campaign -- concluded: "The polarized debate makes it very difficult to build coalition majorities," he concluded.
